strengths: The task is well motivated: combining a reference image with a description of changed appearance addresses a useful gap between image-based and text-based person retrieval. Learning without composed-query training triplets is practically attractive.

ITCPR is a potentially useful benchmark contribution, containing 2,202 queries, 2,225 annotated triplets, and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three datasets. Manual relative-caption annotation and additional screening for false negatives are worthwhile efforts.

Results demonstrate substantial gains over simple fusion with the same fine-tuned encoders. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.91% Rank-1 and 55.63% mAP, versus 32.02% and 41.83% for image–text feature averaging in Table I.

The framework is straightforward and supported by clear diagrams, loss definitions, and substantial training details. Experiments cover two backbone sizes, supervision variants, training-data quantities, mapper architectures, and inference costs.
weaknesses: The central comparison with prior methods is confounded. Table I and Section V-B indicate that Pic2Word and SEARLE retain inversion networks trained against original CLIP while being evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This can introduce an encoder–mapper mismatch that disadvantages these baselines. Retraining the closest methods with the same person-domain data and frozen fine-tuned encoders is necessary to establish the claimed methodological improvement.

Methodological originality is limited beyond the task and benchmark. Mapping image features into pseudo-word tokens for composed retrieval is already central to Pic2Word and SEARLE, while the encoder adaptation uses established person-retrieval objectives. Caption-based inversion supervision is a sensible extension, but its reported advantage over visual supervision is comparatively modest: 45.55% versus 43.96% Rank-1 with ViT-L/14. The current comparisons do not establish how much improvement requires the proposed changes rather than domain adaptation.

Evaluation independence is insufficiently documented. ITCPR is described as exclusively a test set, yet its results guide mapper depth, width, and prompt selection in Figure 7 and Table V. No separate validation set or independent model-selection procedure is reported, creating a risk of optimistic test performance. Repeated-run uncertainty is also absent, limiting interpretation of small ablation and ensemble gains.

The benchmark needs stronger characterization to support broad claims. Evaluation is confined to one curated collection centered on clothing changes, without results broken down by source or modification type. False-negative correction uses encoder-based candidate retrieval, but candidate coverage, annotation agreement, and audit results are unspecified. Consequently, label completeness and generalization beyond this collection remain uncertain.

The intended person-search applications and reuse of identifiable imagery warrant documentation of dataset reuse and redistribution permissions, privacy considerations, and potential surveillance misuse. These are not addressed in the manuscript. The decisive concerns for my recommendation, however, are the uncontrolled comparisons and unclear test-set independence, which outweigh the promising benchmark and reported gains.
